お雪.cast: The heroine, and the one wholly invented character in the book: an Edo-born samurai widow living alone in Kyoto, a painter, who becomes Toshizō's one love.
お雪.note: Oyuki (given name Yuki) is Shiba’s invention; see the note at her first appearance. She recurs to the end of the novel as the woman who draws out Toshizō’s private self.

加田進次郎.note: Oyuki’s late husband in the novel, an Edo-resident foot-guard of the Ōgaki domain; like Oyuki, a fictional figure.

大垣.note: A fudai castle-town and domain in Mino (modern Gifu), ‘Ōgaki of the guns’ (see ch25).

田中光顕.note: Tanaka Mitsuaki (1843–1939), a Tosa loyalist who after the Restoration became a count and Imperial Household Minister; Shiba quotes his recollection of fearing the Shinsengumi.

十津川.note: A mountain district of Yamato (modern Nara) whose rural samurai were fierce imperial loyalists; see the note here.

吉田良道.note: The Kyoto painter under whom the fictional Oyuki is said to study; part of Shiba’s invented history for her.

ch32.note: The Totsukawa-gō was a mountain district of Yamato (modern Nara) whose gōshi, or rural samurai, held in return for old service a rare exemption from tax and a fierce, hereditary loyalty to the Emperor. Many came up to Kyōto as the Restoration neared — Totsukawa men had risen with the Tenchūgumi in 1863 — which is why one of them stands here among Shichiri’s hired swords.

Tanaka Mitsuaki (1843–1939), a Tosa loyalist who after the Restoration rose to count and Imperial Household Minister and made himself the great collector of the Restoration men’s records. Shiba breaks his own narrative to quote Tanaka’s recollection — the enemy’s own testimony to how the mere sight of Hijikata scattered the young loyalists — a real memoir set down in old age, long after the event.

A gandō was a hand-lantern with its candle hung in gimbals inside a hooded metal barrel, so that it stayed lit at any angle and threw its beam one way only, like a bull’s-eye lamp — the night-fighter’s and the housebreaker’s light.

ch32.anchor: the left-mitsudomoe crest on Toshizō's right sleeve
ch32.note: The mitsudomoe is a whirl of three comma-shapes, an old and common device; the ‘left’ form turns one way, the ‘right’ the other. This left-mitsudomoe was the Hijikata family crest. That the dead husband’s clothes Oyuki later brings out bear the very same crest is the quiet omen Shiba sets at their meeting.

None of this is history. Oyuki is Shiba’s one wholly invented character, created to give Toshizō a private life the record does not supply, and so a door into the man’s inward self. The point is stated outright in this edition’s back matter, in the commentary by the director of the 2020 film; Shiba’s own afterword speaks only of Hijikata. The circumstantial detail — the art-name Kōka, the surviving paintings, the teacher Yoshida Ryōdō, the Ōgaki husband — is the novelist’s craft, not fact: there was no historical Oyuki. She recurs to the end of the book.
